title: What If a Fart Was Your Only Rocket in Space? 🚀
description:
Gus is stuck floating in space, ten feet from his ship, with nothing to push on. He had beans for lunch, so he tries the only rocket he has. This is how far it gets him, and what gets him home.

The numbers:
• One fart is about 90 millilitres of gas (the median in the one study that measured it; range 33 to 125). At body temperature that is about a tenth of a gram
• Nobody has published a measured exit speed. We assume the popular figure of 10 feet a second, which is also what 90 ml leaving in one second through a small opening gives, and we assume all of it leaves straight backwards
• Gus (180 lb) plus a spacewalk suit (about 280 lb) is 460 lb. Conservation of momentum: 0.1 g at 10 ft/s moves 460 lb at 1.5 millionths of a metre per second, about 90 micrometres a minute, the width of a human hair. Ten feet takes 23.6 days. The suit's main air supply lasts about 8 hours, enough for 1.7 inches
• A half-pound slipper thrown at 20 mph gives him 1 centimetre a second: ten feet in 5 minutes 13 seconds. That is 6,500 times the push of the fart
• And a spacesuit is airtight, so in real life the gas never leaves and the push is exactly zero
(Real spacewalkers wear a small nitrogen jet pack called SAFER for exactly this: 3 lb of gas, good for about 10 feet a second. Our formula gives the same order for it.)

Sources:
• Tomlin, Lowis and Read, "Investigation of normal flatus production in healthy volunteers", Gut 32, 665 (1991)
• NASA, Extravehicular Mobility Unit fact sheets (suit mass, 8-hour primary life support); NASA, Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER)
• B. Ley, "Diameter of a Human Hair", The Physics Factbook (17 to 181 micrometres)
• Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, any mechanics textbook

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
